Alternative fuels such as methanol and ethanol have a near-zero cetane number; instead, they have high research octane numbers (a measure of resistance to auto-ignite or knock in a spark-ignited engine). Types of combustion systems and ability to retrofit existing locomotive engines in the near term to help meet the sector’s emission reduction goals are described in Huang et al. (2025). A 2030 design case was summarized for near-term uses of alternative fuels in locomotives, in which the first consideration went to fuels that are compatible with current diesel engine fueling and combustion systems (also referred to as drop-in fuels) or can be used with retrofit solutions. For modern turbocharged, direct-injection 4-stroke diesel engines, the fuels of interest in this project can be grouped based on whether they are drop-in replacements. Drop-in or near-drop-in replacements require no—or minimal—retrofit technologies to store the fuel in existing diesel tanks, use the existing high-pressure fuel delivery system (high-pressure fuel pumps and high- pressure direct injectors), and are compatible with the combustion geometry of the piston and quiescent in-cylinder flow fields. Dual-fuel techniques use a direct injection of a high-cetane fuel as the ignition source for a premixed charge of another fuel that can either be port-injected (a port fuel injector located in the intake manifold or upstream) or have two direct injectors. The commercial implementation of dual- fuel natural gas locomotive uses a port injection, diesel ignition strategy. There is a limit to how much diesel displacement can be achieved with a port fuel injection dual fuel strategy, because the fuel displaces air coming into the cylinder, which is needed to provide oxygen to the combustion event. 21 Spark ignition for volatile, high-octane fuels (ethanol, methanol etc.) is not currently implemented in commercial freight locomotives, but its use is well established for light-duty and medium-duty vehicles. Prechamber spark-ignition is widely used in stationary power applications and more recently as pre-commercial technology for vehicles from companies like MAHLE and others. The conventional diesel combustion strategy requires no changes or minimal changes to the fueling system and represents the most straightforward path to implementing alternative fuels. Dual-fuel strategies require some level retrofit technologies for the engine and the onboard fuel systems to implement. The simplest dual-fuel retrofit strategy is to keep the direct injection diesel fueling system in place and modify the intake manifold to incorporate port fuel injectors. This also requires the addition of a second fuel tank and fueling system. With this port-injection dual-fuel strategy, the diesel combustion system can be left in place for backwards compatibility if the locomotive needs to refuel at a depot that does not carry the alternative fuel. Other dual-fuel systems including using a high-pressure direct injection system or two direct injectors would require a redesign of the cylinder head and the addition of a second high-pressure fuel delivery system. Dual-fuel strategies offer a range of flexibility specific combustion strategies and amounts of diesel displacement.
